title: If 2
subtitle: Had they not rushed Jo to hospital ... / if you happen to ...
summary: Drop if and invert with should, were and had, know when if ... will is possible, use if ... happen to for unlikely events, and make comparisons with as if.

lesson.heading: Leaving out if: should, were, had
lesson.text: When the first verb in a conditional if-clause is **should**, **were** or **had**, we can leave out *if* and put the verb at the start of the clause. This is formal or literary, and only happens in hypothetical conditionals - the ones that answer 'What would happen if ...?'

examples.text: **Should** any of this cost you anything, send me the bill.
examples.note: = If any of this should cost ...

examples.text: It would be embarrassing, **were** she to find out the truth.
examples.note: = ... if she were to find out ...

examples.text: **Had** they not rushed Jo to hospital, she would have died.

left.label: Possible - the if-clause is the result of the main clause
examples: Open a window **if it will help** you to sleep.
'Helping you to sleep' is the result of opening the window (or ... if it helps you to sleep).

right.label: Not possible - no result relationship
examples: I will be angry **if it turns out** that you are wrong.
not ... if it will turn out that you are wrong

lesson.heading: if ... will in requests
lesson.text: We also use **if ... will** in requests, with the meaning 'if you are willing to'. **If ... would** is more polite.

examples.text: **If you will** / **would** take your seats, ladies and gentlemen, we can begin the meeting.

lesson.heading: if ... will for disapproval; if ... won't for a refusal
lesson.text: In real conditionals we can use **if ... will** to show that we disapprove of something. In speech *will* is stressed. **If ... won't** talks about a refusal to do something.

examples.text: *A:* I'm tired. *B:* Well, if you **will** go to bed so late, I'm not surprised.
There's no point in trying to teach the class **if they won't** pay attention.

lesson.heading: if ... happen to; if ... should
lesson.text: In a real conditional we use **if ... happen to**, **if ... should** or **if ... should happen to** for something that may be possible but is not very likely. *If ... happen to* is the most common in speech.

examples.text: **If you happen to** be in our area, drop in and see us.
examples.note: or If you should (happen to) be ...

lesson.note: We don't use this pattern in unreal conditionals about states or events the speaker sees as highly unlikely or impossible: If the North Sea froze in winter, you could walk from London to Oslo. (but probably not If the North Sea happened to freeze ...)

lesson.heading: as if in comparison clauses
lesson.text: In comparison clauses **as if** can be followed by a noun phrase, an -ing clause, a past participle clause or a to-infinitive. We use it to explain something, or to say that something appears to be the case but is not.

examples.text: Magnus walked in **as if** nothing had happened.
His hands made a circular motion, **as if steering** a bus through a sharp bend.
When he caught the ball, Lee fell to the floor **as if hit** by a bullet.
**As if to convince** herself that Luis was really there, she gently touched his cheek.

lesson.heading: as though and like
lesson.text: We can use **as though** instead of as if. In informal speech some people use **like** with the same meaning.

examples.text: The crowd reacted **as though** they were watching a boxing match.
He walked into the room **like** nothing had happened.

lesson.text: Inversion only works with should, were and had - you cannot drop if in front of any other verb.

exercises.prompt: ___ the symptoms remain 72 hours after starting the course of medicine, consult your doctor again.
exercises.explanation: Should + subject replaces if ... should in formal instructions.

exercises.prompt: ___ Clare's friends still living in Brussels, she would have been able to stay with them.
exercises.explanation: if they were still living becomes Were they still living, with if dropped.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite 'You would know what you have to do for homework, if you had not been absent from school on Friday' beginning with Had.
exercises.answer: Had you not been absent from school on Friday, you would know what you have to do for homework.
exercises.explanation: if you had not been absent inverts to Had you not been absent.

exercises.statement: If I will press this button, will it start to record?
exercises.explanation: If I press this button, will it start to record? Pressing the button is not the result of the recording, so if ... will is not possible.

exercises.statement: You're welcome to borrow my old bike, if you think it will be of any use to you.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Being of use is the result of borrowing the bike, so if ... will works.

exercises.prompt: I will be angry if it ___ that you are wrong.
exercises.explanation: There is no result relationship here, so we use the present simple after if.

exercises.statement: If you'll complain about me, I'll get into trouble with my teacher.
exercises.explanation: If you complain about me, I'll get into trouble with my teacher. Your complaining is not the result of my getting into trouble.

exercises.statement: If he won't resign, the Prime Minister should sack him.
exercises.explanation: Correct. if ... won't talks about a refusal to do something.

exercises.prompt: If you ___ see Georgia when I'm in Rome, I'll send her your regards.
exercises.explanation: if ... happen to marks something that is possible but not very likely.

exercises.prompt: Can the if-clause be rewritten with happen to, or is the situation too unlikely for that pattern?
categories: Too unlikely - keep the past simple

items.text: If I see Georgia when I'm in Rome, I'll send her your regards.
The plan for a new airport outside London is bad news if you live nearby.
If you are in the south of Spain next week, there is a good chance of seeing a total eclipse of the sun.
If a UFO landed in the centre of New York, there would be mass panic.
If I was the President, I would order our nuclear weapons to be destroyed.
If the North Sea froze in winter, you could walk from London to Oslo.

exercises.prompt: Match each action with the as if clause that explains it.

pairs.right: as if I had said something shocking.

pairs.left: He folded his arms on the table and laid his head on them,
pairs.right: as if overcome with a great weariness.

pairs.left: She stared hard at the parcel
pairs.right: as if trying to imagine what it contained.
as if to agree with everything Julia said.

pairs.left: The back of the car looked
pairs.right: as if it had been reversed into a wall.

exercises.prompt: When he caught the ball, Lee fell to the floor as if ___ by a bullet.
exercises.explanation: As if can be followed by a past participle clause with no subject or auxiliary.
